system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2145-12-13 04:28:00 to 2145-12-14 15:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of ankylosing spondylitis, severe obesity, hypertension, asthma, and obstructive sleep apnea, was admitted for acute on chronic left lower back and sacroiliac pain rated 10/10. He reported symptoms typical of prior flares and requested prednisone and opioids for relief. Evaluation revealed mild elevation in inflammatory markers (CRP 12.4, ESR 38) but no signs of infection or acute pathology. Rheumatology and chronic pain consultations did not support steroid use, instead recommending NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, and physical therapy, all of which the patient declined due to prior side effects or concerns. His home pain regimen, including oxycodone and oxycontin, was continued, and tizanidine was increased to 4 mg BID PRN. The patient expressed dissatisfaction but agreed to follow up with rheumatology to discuss restarting biologic therapy pending infectious workup results. He was discharged home in stable condition after two days with plans for outpatient follow-up.
problems: Ankylosing spondylitis of unspecified sites in spine
Morbid (severe) obesity due to excess calories

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you came in with trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been having a lot of shortness of breath. I can’t even walk up the stairs without stopping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And when did this start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started after my Simponi infusion. I got chest tightness and a cough, like I’ve had before. Then seven days ago, I spiked a fever—up to 102.7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what happened after the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The fever went away after two days with prednisone and azithromycin, but my cough and breathing got worse. I’m using my nebulizer six times a day and can’t sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You were given albuterol and ceftriaxone in the ER. We’re admitting you because your asthma flare isn’t improving with outpatient treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had asthma for years, but this feels worse than usual. I use albuterol before exercise, but I don’t always use my other inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ll help you get through this flare. Your chest X-ray didn’t show pneumonia, but there’s some mild atelectasis in the bases—likely from not being able to take deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s an asthma exacerbation triggered by a recent upper respiratory infection. Your labs are mostly normal—white count is 8.9, no signs of severe infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had to stop past TNF inhibitors because of infections. I’m worried about Simponi.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear that concern. But your rheumatologist feels the benefits outweigh the risks, and your breathing has improved since restarting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I guess. What’s the plan now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your prednisone at 60 mg daily, give you duoneb treatments every six hours, and monitor your breathing. You’re on room air with 94% oxygen, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on levofloxacin, but I didn’t want to continue it—side effects bother me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ve switched you to Augmentin for two more days to finish the antibiotic course, since you were already on azithromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s better. I’ve had bad reactions to other antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on that. For now, rest and let the nebulizers do their work. We’ll check on you regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning again. How are you feeling after your first night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I slept a bit more. The nebulizers are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your breathing sounds improved—less wheezing. We’ll keep up the duonebs and steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely two days. We want to make sure your breathing keeps improving before sending you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been in before for pain, but this is different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this admission is for your asthma, not pain. We’ll continue your home pain meds—oxycontin and breakthrough oxycodone—as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using Toradol in the past for pain—can I have that if needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can use Toradol for breakthrough pain, yes. But you’re allergic to NSAIDs, so we’ll be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I forgot—NSAIDs, methadone, Lyrica, gabapentin. I’ve had bad reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted all your allergies. You’re safe here. Let’s focus on getting your lungs better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your breathing is much better. You’re speaking in full sentences, no distress, and your lungs are clearer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. I can breathe deeper now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ll finish Augmentin for two more days and continue prednisone at 60 mg for two more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then you’ll taper the prednisone by 10 mg each day until it’s done. Keep using albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular inhalers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once this flare settles, go back to your usual budesonide and albuterol. Try to use them more consistently—they help prevent flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I’ll follow up with my PCP too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, keep using your CPAP for sleep apnea—it helps your breathing overall. And take omeprazole for your GERD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually do. I know they matter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re doing well. You can go home now. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call your doctor if breathing worsens. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your time getting up. Nurse will assist you with discharge paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep monitoring your breathing. If you need your nebulizer more than usual, don’t wait—seek care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And follow up with your PCP within a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll schedule that today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of ankylosing spondylitis on Simponi, exercise-induced asthma, chronic pain, GERD, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnea, was admitted for an asthma exacerbation triggered by an upper respiratory infection. He presented with worsening shortness of breath, cough, and increased nebulizer use despite outpatient treatment with prednisone and azithromycin. His fever had resolved, but respiratory symptoms progressed, prompting hospitalization. He was treated with IV ceftriaxone initially, transitioned to Augmentin, continued on prednisone 60 mg daily, and received duoneb treatments. His breathing improved significantly, and he was discharged home after two days with instructions to complete antibiotics, taper prednisone by 10 mg daily, and resume home asthma medications as the flare resolved. Follow-up with his primary care provider was advised.
problems: Ankylosing spondylitis of unspecified sites in spine
